speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I thank the various Members who spoke last week, in particular, for each of their support of the Ministry of Law's (MinLaw's) work.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 1826, the Second Charter of Justice formally established the Court of Judicature of Singapore, at that time, a fledgling colonial legal order in a trading post that had barely found its footing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The law then served a different purpose, a different master and in a very different age.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nearly two centuries on, what Singapore has built has been nothing short of remarkable.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We now rank among the top legal and intellectual property (IP) systems in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our Courts and dispute resolution institutions, like the Singapore International Arbitration Centre, Singapore International Mediation Centre and Singapore International Commercial Court, are globally recognised for excellence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Whilst our legal beginnings were inherited, we have since moulded and contextualised the rule of law to serve our nation and our people.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This has been the Singapore story of progress.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Generations of lawyers, judges, academics and policy-makers understood that a rules-based society is the bedrock upon which everything else – commerce, safety and liberty – is built.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will therefore have to redouble efforts to keep our laws updated and relevant and also be bold and open to embracing changes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw will continue to press on with reform and progress in our legal policies.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In my speech this morning, I will set out our overarching vision, the priority areas that we will focus on as well as outline some of the key challenges that we will have to confront.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue our work to build Singapore as a legal and professional services hub.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are powerful growth engines, providing opportunities, driving economic expansion and job creation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Beyond reviewing legislation, we will also identify opportunities in emerging areas.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This includes supporting the green transition, the digital economy and major regional infrastructure projects, as well as sports and entertainment dispute resolution that Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Beyond domestic reforms, Singapore will continue to contribute to international thought leadership.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: By being present in the global legal mindshare, we ensure that we will not merely be price-takers but we will actively play a role in shaping the law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Singapore Convention on Mediation bears our name, our country’s name – a testament to our involvement in shaping international dispute resolution.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Indeed, Singaporeans also contribute to leadership on the international stage, including Mr Daren Tang and Ambassador Rena Lee, as mentioned by Mr Christopher de Souza.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our international engagement also extends to strengthening legal cooperation frameworks with our partners, ensuring that as commerce and cross-border activity grow, the rule of law keeps pace.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government will also similarly ratify the AET once we have completed our own internal procedures.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the risks to Singaporeans, there are robust legal safeguards in the AET, which set out the circumstances where extradition will not be granted.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One example is if the request is made to prosecute the fugitive based on his race, religion, nationality or political opinions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we must continue to cultivate a strong legal profession.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is the backbone of our legal progress.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we want Singapore to remain a jurisdiction where the finest legal minds choose to practise here and where homegrown talent is given every opportunity to flourish and remain at the core of our profession.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I encourage our law firms to expand their horizons, think about internationalising their practices.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Given our market, Singapore’s size, we must build our legal ecosystem with the broader Asia and ASEAN in context.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the case for doing so is compelling.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In ASEAN alone, it is set as a bloc to become the fourth largest economy by 2030, if not sooner.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And foreign direct investments into ASEAN have been steadily rising.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, I believe our firms are well-primed to capture these opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, we recognise the value that foreign law firms and lawyers bring to our industry and the wider economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Cassandra Lee mentioned balancing between open competitiveness and preserving a Singapore core.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore, in fact, has gradually liberalised the legal sector since the 1990s, and we have not changed our posture.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They complement our Singapore lawyers, offering advice and expertise on international and foreign law, which we need as a global business hub.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Indeed, over the same period of time, since the year 2000, our legal services exports have gone up eight-fold, which shows that when we bring it together – foreign lawyers, Singapore practitioners at the core – we can extract value.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We regularly review our frameworks to remain attractive to foreign law firms and lawyers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, Sir, we will redouble efforts to develop the individual lawyer.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The strength of any legal system and indeed, of our legal profession, lies ultimately in the strength of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will therefore expand education and competency frameworks, not just in technical skills but in civil law, technology literacy and cross-border practice, so that every Singapore lawyer can serve their clients and their community with confidence and competence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This also means confronting the sustainability of legal practice, issues which Ms Kuah Boon Theng, Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Cassandra Lee spoke on.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And in fact, the number of Singapore lawyers in practice grew 26% over the past decade.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, over the last 10 years, the number of lawyers in practice grew 26%.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nonetheless, I agree with the observations made by the hon Members.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We must continue to explore ways to alleviate pressures on our lawyers in light of the changing environment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Ms Kuah has noted, the challenges are multi-faceted.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will require collective effort, including law firms, which will set the conditions for growth, exposure and mentorship for lawyers, but also lawyers themselves, each of them, who can be stewards of their own careers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will have to think collectively and carefully about embracing technology to automate mundane tasks, equipping lawyers with relevant 21st century skills, widening the industry ecosystem, so that lawyers can pursue diverse interests and strengths, and find meaning, purpose and value in the profession that they practise in.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Minister of State Murali Pillai will share our efforts on education and the adoption of legaltech.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Law Society and the Singapore Academy of Law have introduced mentorship programmes and other initiatives to help promote sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Committee will explore these matters, from the holistic perspective of ensuring the long-term sustainability of our legal sector.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In parallel, the Government will also continue to support in-house counsel, who are integral to Singapore’s legal ecosystem and economic competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Vikram Nair noted, lawyers joining in-house legal teams are not a loss.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in that period of time, while our industry has remained stable, in fact, with a 26% increase, the number of in-house counsel has more than doubled over the last 10 years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It reflects growth in not just the number of lawyers in practice or in in-house counsel roles but the growth of MNCs in Singapore, which supports the economy, in turn requiring in-house counsel legal support.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In-house counsel help companies navigate regulatory landscapes and invest with confidence in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, Sir, let me turn to enhancing access to justice, ensuring that those who are most vulnerable and most in need can still access our first-class legal system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, we have shifted away from the adversarial approach in family proceedings, addressing non-compliance with maintenance orders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have strengthened the management of community disputes through mandatory mediation and we support those with special needs in our criminal justice system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also made a firm commitment to Government legal aid through the Legal Aid Bureau and the setting up of the Public Defender’s Office.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have continued to work with the legal fraternity and partners like Pro Bono SG to deliver legal aid and expand outreach and assistance through schemes like the Community Law Centres.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have introduced technology, such as LawGoWhere, to bring legal services closer to Singaporeans and help them to navigate the process and empower and enable self-help.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This year, Sir, we will make another shift to expand civil legal aid coverage.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This would cover more households, allowing them to benefit from legal advice in the appropriate cases.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When we did a survey, we found that between the previous threshold of $1,050 and $1,650, about half of civil litigants in this expanded income range remain unrepresented.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some may have done so by choice, but after we put this in place, we will allow them to now avail themselves of legal aid, should that become necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will extend more legal aid to more Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric will share more details on these efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, I turn to optimising our state assets and I thank Mr de Souza for recognising our efforts over the years to unlock underutilised spaces for social and community good, place-making, such as providing arts spaces for practitioners and sports and recreational facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric will share how SLA continues to support our economic and social needs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At this juncture, let me turn to address Ms Sylvia Lim's cut on the appointment of the Attorney-General (AG).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim's cut was originally filed to the Prime Minister's Office.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It was redirected to MinLaw, as I will respond on behalf of the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Ms Lim noted, Mr Wong has had a distinguished legal career.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prior to his appointment, he grew and led Singapore's largest law firm and was widely regarded as the country's top corporate lawyer over many years, with an international standing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, I would say that his reputation stands as amongst the best in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As AG, Mr Wong has made major contributions across almost every area of law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under his leadership, the AGC has advised the Government on complex legal and constitutional matters; prosecuted criminal offences fairly and firmly; and ensured that legislation introduced in Parliament is clear, sound and fit for Singapore's purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: His experience and steady hand have also been especially valuable to Singapore in sensitive international matters, some of which are presently ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim, in her speech, has described the appointment process for the AG as "thin", if I heard her correctly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But I would have to disagree and would instead characterise it quite differently.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is a clear, deliberate and very structured process of appointment, with the appropriate checks and balances.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It involves consultation with the head of the Judiciary, the leadership of the PSC and the elected President exercising his constitutional role, in consultation with the CPA, before the AG is either appointed or renewed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This process reflects a careful and considered balance between executive responsibility and institutional safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim then goes on to suggest that there should be public disclosure of these deliberations.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, these are matters for Chairman PSC and the CPA to assess independently and take a considered view of.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The CPA, for instance, does not publish its advice to the President, nor is the Government privy to its deliberations.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, confidential deliberations also serve an important function when it comes to making such appointments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If you put it out publicly, you put the candidates out for public debate.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Even the best of candidates will have some detractors; a small minority, but there will be some.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Suitable candidates may well then be deterred from even being considered if discussions as to their suitability and perhaps their rejection were to be made publicly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The consultation process also requires candour and frank assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is easy to say, let us have more information, let us have more public debate, public discourse and deliberations.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we have seen other countries using such methods in other systems.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the question we have to ask ourselves is, are they better?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore's legal system, our corruption levels, our adherence to the rule of law has consistently been marked internationally very well and I think we want to continue with this.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In some jurisdictions, the AGs are elected office holders, but Singapore has had a different model since our Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He is appointed based on professional excellence, integrity and judgement.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The safeguards, however, lie in the constitutional requirements and qualifications required, the consultative process that I have just outlined and ultimately, in the performance and the conduct of the office.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim also says that there are many qualified persons for the position.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That may be so, if one considers only the basic eligibility criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, the selection of an AG is not simply about meeting the basic criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It requires a careful assessment of who is best suited to discharge the heavy and very important responsibilities of the office.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We want the best, not just those who might qualify.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What then does the Government look for in an AG?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I said, the role of an AG is a demanding one.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is, in fact, one of the most critical offices in our constitutional framework.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, beyond formal qualification, it calls for an individual of high professional standing, wide-ranging legal experience, sound judgement and a strong sense of public duty.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The AG must also have unimpeachable integrity and strong moral fibre.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He must render objective advice and act fairly in the conduct of prosecutions, even when doing so may be difficult or unpopular.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He must be prepared to uphold the law impartially and apply it equally to everyone, whether one is a Minister or the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Individuals with the requisite experience, judgement and integrity for this office are not easily found.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government continually looks out for suitable candidates, one who can shoulder the full weight of these responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, in making any appointments, the Government also takes into account a range of considerations, including the performance of the incumbent, his ability and willingness to serve and whether there are significant ongoing matters that require continuity and careful oversight.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In particular, the Government continues to rely on Mr Wong's counsel on significant matters that remain in progress today, including negotiations on maritime boundaries; tax and financial sector legal reforms; and complex cross-border criminal matters.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These and others are substantial responsibilities that will benefit from deep expertise, sound judgement and a steady hand.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Wong has had a proven track record.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have seen and worked with him, we have assessed and we know the quality of the work, including on sensitive matters.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I believe this is a system of appointment which is careful, structured and designed to preserve both independence and public trust.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My colleagues, Senior Minister of State Murali and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua will set out further details in their speeches.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, even as we pursue these priorities, we must be very clear-eyed about the challenges that lie ahead of us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are entering into an era of profound disruption, the kind of disruption the legal industry has not encountered in recent memory.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the most consequential driver of this disruption is artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That is just about a year and a half, two years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Closer to home, Singapore law firms, some with MinLaw's support, have begun piloting AI tools.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This and other examples, many other examples, shows a profession already in motion, moving and evolving with the advent of technology.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we have to ask ourselves, what does this mean for us, as a legal profession, in practice?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: AI-powered tools are already conducting document reviews, drafting contracts and flagging regulatory exposure across multiple jurisdictions at speeds that no humans can replicate or even match.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some platforms can even analyse thousands of precedents and generate predictive assessments of case outcomes – work that previously demanded years and years of legal experience.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But they also raise very important questions for the future of our profession.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: How does a young lawyer develop judgement, intuition and professional instinct if the AI performs the basic tasks and gives the answers to these young lawyers?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: How will our lawyers develop these instincts which are honed by a process of doing and redoing and repeating it?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Who bears responsibility when the AI produces errors with commercial implications?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: How do we regulate cross-border AI-generated advice without, at the same time, allowing regulation to stifle innovation?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And perhaps most fundamentally, how do we harness AI to serve the public interest, and not just allow it to widen the gap between those who can afford sophisticated legal technology and those who cannot?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The impact on legal education is equally pressing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our law schools have, for generations, trained lawyers through a well-established pedagogy, where the process of reading and analysing cases, drafting legal memos and crafting oral arguments – all of these, which I described as the process – is as important as the outcome when it comes to training.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But if the AI can do the research or draft a memo in minutes, what happens to this training?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What happens to the cultivation of hands-on experience, in making mistakes?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Perhaps the law degree ought then to redouble its emphasis on what AI cannot replicate.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ethical reasoning, empathetic client engagement and the exercise of judgement in areas of genuine ambiguity and moral courage.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The challenge is equally acute for those who are already in practice and in continuing legal education.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Can our structures support a landscape where skills need to be updated every once in a while, more recently, every once in a few months?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These questions, Sir, do not admit easy answers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They go to the heart of what it means to practise law, to train lawyers and to uphold the standards of a profession entrusted with the heavy responsibility of the administration of justice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are not matters which any single institution can resolve in isolation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The challenges before us will require a collective response – from practitioners, in-house counsel, academics, regulators, policy-makers, law students as well as members of the public whose interests the legal system ultimately serves.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is an opportunity for an open, frank and candid conversation about the challenges we face, starting with AI and technology, but also understanding the road ahead and the opportunities that might lie ahead for us and the future we want to build, collectively, for Singapore's legal industry.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What you do matters a lot, not just to the profession, but to Singapore's development and our continued success.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In this extraordinary age of change, perhaps it matters more.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore did not build our legal system by accident, as I sketched out earlier, nor can we hope to preserve and strengthen it by accident.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will require all of us – my Ministry, the Bar, the Judiciary, our law schools, the firms and every single lawyer – to engage with purpose and genuine commitment and intentionality to tackling the disruptive challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that is work that we must continue together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Chairman, the law cannot generate a single cent in commerce or bring a single idea into market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It powers neither our economy nor our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It collapses on itself when it stands alone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Yet, we will have no peace, no security, no comfort, neither prosperity nor progress without the law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The law underwrites both the private and the public sectors of our world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Today, I will speak about both and how they, together, secure the livelihoods of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: First, intangible assets (IA) and IP are critical for enterprises to develop – as mentioned by the hon Members Mr Jackson Lam and Mr Mark Lee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The most valuable resources of a business are often intangible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: These assets are generated by the ingenuity and creativity of men, but they are given specific value by the law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Singapore has been working for decades to harness IP for economic growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Since 2021, the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) has stepped up to attract and grow innovative enterprises using IA and IP, guided by the Singapore IP Strategy (SIPS) 2030.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: While the assets may be intangible, the benefits of focusing on IA and IP are tangible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This year, IPOS celebrates 25 years of empowering businesses to turn ideas into tangible assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In the second tranche of SIPS 2030, we will work harder to uplift enterprises and strengthen Singapore as a global IA and IP Hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This includes – first, supporting businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs), in managing their IP and unlocking its value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: From there, more SMEs will gain access to initiatives like WIPO's IP Management Clinic Singapore programme to develop IP strategies and overseas expansion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Second, stepping up work on IA and IP valuation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This includes developing frameworks with financial institutions, public agencies and industry partners, to help companies realise IA value and commercialise their ideas through licensing and partnerships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: To Mr Mark Lee's queries on research attachments as well as IP financing – on the former, the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) seconds researchers to SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: IPI Singapore, a subsidiary under Enterprise Singapore, also assists SMEs with technology matching services and advisory support to develop go-to-market strategies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: On the latter, IPOS is studying the market gaps in enterprise financing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Human creativity is the lifeblood of innovation and progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As we harness AI for growth, we are committed to maintaining a balanced and robust IP regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Ms Goh Hanyan and Mr Jackson Lam spoke about concerns relating to the training and use of generative AI (GenAI), particularly from the creative sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Our approach to developing our IP regime is human-centric.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are working with stakeholders to refine our regime, for example, the Singapore Academy of Law (SAL) supported by MinLaw and IPOS, organised industry and expert roundtables.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The feedback was broadly supportive of Singapore's copyright framework which balances AI development with guardrails to protect rights-holders' interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It also raised suggestions for further consultation and refinement, which we will study.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Last year, IPOS also launched explainers to help the public and businesses understand how copyright laws address key GenAI issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are monitoring international developments to remain competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This aims to engage broader perspectives and co-create our approach to AI-related IP issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Businesses need clear, reliable and impartial pathways to resolution, providing predictability and certainty in their relationships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Singapore has long recognised this and worked hard to be an international dispute resolution hub, as hon Members Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Vikram Nair said.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Over the past decades, our ecosystem has deepened.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Our institutions refined their rules and procedures, expanded their international panels and strengthened their case management capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Signature platforms, such as the Singapore Convention Week, reinforce our reputation as a global node.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This contributes to Singapore's standing as a services centre and signals our openness for commerce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: However, the landscape is evolving and we must continue to innovate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Technology is transforming dispute management, from virtual hearings to AI-assisted document review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Our institutions have also deepened offerings in specialist areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MinLaw is working with industry on three thrusts: first, education and professionalisation – to deepen the strength of our legal industry; second, adoption of legaltech – to reduce repetitive, low-value tasks; and third, providing opportunities in emerging areas of work, such as the environmental, social and governance (ESG) sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We have been implementing recommendations of the Reform of Legal Education Working Group since late 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: These better equip legal professionals for cross-border work with civil law partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: By 2027, a framework and training roadmap for allied legal professionals will follow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Hon Members Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Cassandra Lee spoke on AI adoption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MinLaw is committed to supporting our legal professionals adopt AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: First, we are addressing the adoption barriers directly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Their experiences will guide how we will support the broader industry in 2027.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will be publishing the Guide in the coming weeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: On Ms Lee's point about AI skills, we are also partnering the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) to build AI fluency amongst our lawyers and in-house counsel through upskilling and training initiatives, together with professional bodies including SAL and the Singapore Corporate Counsel Association (SCCA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Third, we are creating more avenues for lawyers, including in-house counsel, to discover legaltech, through initiatives such as LegalTech GoWhere and the Singapore Open Legal Informatics Database (SOLID) with our partner, the Singapore Management University.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Besides assisting legal professionals, AI can transform the way our society interacts with the law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This has tremendous potential for good – provided it is harnessed responsibly, as hon Member Mr Nair mentioned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Users ultimately remain responsible for how they use these tools and the attendant risks – knowing that the algorithms are incapable of weighing consequences or applying ethical reasoning in the way legal professionals do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MinLaw will monitor these developments and raise public awareness on the responsible use of GenAI tools in legal matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: My final point is on capturing opportunities in emerging areas of legal demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: One example is ESG, which Ms Gho Sze Kee spoke on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Sustainability is one of the paradoxes of the business world, even as it is one of the most important and consequential factors in business decisions, it is often overlooked or under-considered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Being an emerging area, the Government is taking a targeted approach to build capability across the legal profession.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MinLaw co-funds secondments for lawyers into participating corporations, giving secondees exposure to ESG business contexts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The pilot began in February with a small initial cohort and we will review its outcome later this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Chairman, I have spoken today about the importance of the law in giving value to ideas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I want to end on the need to give power to the law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In a world increasingly dominated by might, money and manipulation, it is vital for us to remember that it is the law that enables justice, reason and rightfulness to find strength and standing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: There are no shortcuts to give power to the law, but one unvarying path is to remember that law is inextricably tied up with the human condition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Even as I spoke about the need for technology, I have spoken more about the need for people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We must build and grow a profession with the skills, courage and moral instincts suited for our tumultuous times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The law underwrites both the private and the public sectors, but it is for, and in the people, that the law finds its surest power.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Chairman, the Rule of Law underpins our society's broader objectives and continued development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In my speech, I will focus on two key areas: first, optimising land and creating good spaces for our economic and social needs; second, upholding the Rule of Law and expanding access to justice to strengthen our social fabric.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We do so by ensuring that no one is denied legal access and by supporting vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This safeguards land resources for our current and future generations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To this end, SLA engages public agencies and industry to better understand market needs and identify opportunities to put state land and properties to good use, in a pro-enterprise manner.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh asked about the use of state land and properties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: SLA has also been activating suitable spaces in response to requests for "weather-proofed" sports spaces.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: One creative example is the placement of sport facilities under viaducts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These were previously under-utilised due to noise and lack of essential utilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But we saw potential in the natural shelter and worked with Sport Singapore to transform the Gali Batu Flyover area into ARK Sports Village @ Segar.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What was previously unused space is now a thriving sports facility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh also asked about a longer tenure for more state properties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Currently, state properties are let out for a range of interim uses, typically with tenures of under 10 years, to retain planning flexibility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Such extended tenure allows time for investment recoupment and greater business certainty.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Ms Goh Han Yan asked about improvements to the Land Betterment Charge (LBC) regime.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We have enhanced various aspects of the LBC framework since it came into force in 2022.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Minister Edwin spoke about the enhancements just last week at the Real Estate Developers' Association of Singapore (REDAS) Spring Festival Lunch.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: More details may be found in his speech on the MinLaw website.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is also vital that our legal processes and frameworks remain accessible, fair and effective.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We continue to review our legal frameworks to adapt to trends and societal needs so that Singaporeans can seek recourse and resolve frictions whenever they arise.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Legislation was passed in 2024 to enhance the Community Disputes Management Framework.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We have made mediation mandatory in appropriate cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Second, a new Community Relations Unit (CRU) has been created to investigate neighbour disputes and to act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Third, we have enhanced the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal (CDRT) to improve the service journey for victims and enable them to obtain relief more quickly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Gerald Giam made several points on the CDRT's processes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Many disputes arise from misunderstandings or lifestyle differences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Calm, neighbourly exchanges can usually go a long way.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But if informal communication fails, parties should attempt formal mediation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mediation at the Community Mediation Centre is quick, effective and free.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The CDRT is an avenue of last resort, after all other measures have failed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As it is a court of law, some proper processes are necessary to ensure the proper administration of justice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The pre-filing assessment is not designed to redirect or deter residents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Instead, it is meant to help residents assess whether their dispute is suitable for the CDRT.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For example, residents should attempt mediation before filing a CDRT claim.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, the form asks whether mediation has been attempted before.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Residents also cannot file a CDRT claim against persons who are not their neighbours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This ensures that residents do not spend time, money and energy filing a claim, that cannot be heard in the CDRT.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Those who need help navigating the e-filing system, including those with specific language needs, can contact the State Courts Service Hub.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: On the $150 filing fee, those with financial need can apply for a waiver.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But again, parties should always attempt mediation first.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Second, we have been studying ways to streamline the enforcement of civil judgments, as mentioned by Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Gabriel Lam and Mr Alex Yeo.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We received feedback that the time, the effort and the cost of enforcing judgments can be disproportionate to the judgment sum, leaving some judgments unenforced.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We have been consulting with relevant stakeholders, including the Bar and the Judiciary, and aim to introduce a Bill later this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We have made changes to help families move forward with minimal acrimony, including addressing non-compliance with maintenance orders, as noted by Mr Nair and Mr Yeo.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This is a good start and we plan to expand coverage in future phases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Another area is ensuring will-making remains accessible to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Depending on complexity, budget and personal preference, they can write their own wills, engage will-making services or even ask a friend for help.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Ms Hany Soh asked if wills can be registered for free in SAL's Wills Registry and suggested regulation or mandatory insurance for non-lawyers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: On the former, the fee defrays the costs of the service, which includes maintaining records for up to 120 years of the testator's life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Those with genuine financial needs can apply for a fee waiver.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I would add that the validity of a will does not depend on registration with the Registry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: On the latter, we do not plan to impose insurance requirements to encourage options for legacy planning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: If the public is unsure whether their service-provider is a licensed lawyer, they may check the MinLaw webpage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It has a search function that lists lawyers who have valid practising licences at the date of the search.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is a key pillar that ensures our laws and justice system are not just for those with means, thereby preserving our social fabric, as mentioned by Mr Nair.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We have been helping those in need through the Legal Aid Bureau (LAB) and the Public Defender's Office (PDO).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Since 1958, LAB has provided the vulnerable with civil legal aid, including matrimonial, monetary claims and probate matters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The impact of LAB's work is significant – receiving an average of around 7,000 applications annually.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In 2022, MinLaw established the PDO, which institutionalised criminal defence aid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A portion of applications is referred to Pro Bono SG's Criminal Legal Aid Scheme under a co-delivery model.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Additionally, LAB and PDO partner with social service agencies, Family Service Centres and Social Services Offices to provide holistic assistance and referrals for applicants with social needs, such as family violence, addiction, mental health and housing problems.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Dr Wan Rizal, Mr Alex Yeo, Mr Gabriel Lam and Mr Jackson Lam asked about ensuring access to legal aid for lower-income and lower-middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We continue to review the means test thresholds regularly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In 2022, we expanded the income coverage for criminal defence aid from the bottom 25th to the bottom 35th percentile by PCHI.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In 2024, we adjusted the PCHI and annual value thresholds for civil legal aid and criminal defence aid, accounting for the increase in household income and property value over the years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We target to implement this later this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Applicants with extenuating circumstances will continue to be reviewed by an independent means test panel comprising legal and social service professionals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Beyond Government schemes, we continue to partner with the legal fraternity and key stakeholders, such as Pro Bono SG to strengthen the legal help ecosystem for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Mr Alex Yeo asked about those facing legal issues arising from the loss of mental capacity of family members.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In 2025, we amended the Legal Aid and Advice Act 1995 to allow means testing based on the mentally incapacitated person, not the volunteers applying to be their deputy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This has reduced financial barriers and encouraged more volunteer deputies for vulnerable persons without family support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In better serving these individuals, we have in the past made some efforts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In 2010, we introduced community-based sentences, including the Mandatory Treatment Order (MTO).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The MTO allows certain offenders with treatable psychiatric conditions to be treated in the community rather than be incarcerated in appropriate cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In 2018, we expanded the MTO scheme to benefit more suitable offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Other measures include the Appropriate Adult Scheme for Persons with Mental Disabilities, administered by MINDS to support such persons during interviews with investigating officers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But we fully recognise that more can be done.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We want to finetune how our system caters to these vulnerable individuals' unique needs while delivering just outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For instance, effective rehabilitation may differ for offenders with different underlying conditions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: While some may benefit from psychiatric treatment, others such as those living with autism or intellectual disability may benefit from other interventions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These questions intersect multiple areas such as law, social services and healthcare, and involve stakeholders from the private and public sector.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Thus, MinLaw formally announced the launch of the Inclusive Justice Taskforce (IJT) in January this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I am privileged to co-lead the IJT alongside Ms Peggy Yee, founding director of PY Legal LLC and a long-time advocate in this space.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Together with our partners, we will press on.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On filing CDRT claims, can vernacular translations be provided on the online application form and can evidence exceeding the two-year limit be allowed to better deal with long-running disputes?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many individuals has the service hub assisted to successfully file applications in each of the last three years?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does the hub provide end-to-end guidance for applicants who are not digitally savvy and not just advice?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, if a resident does not have a Singpass, can the service hub help the resident to complete the filing of the CDRT claim?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: On the provisions of information in vernacular languages on the website, I think that is something that we can potentially explore and look at.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Of course, we are also mindful not to provide for content in a variety of languages such that it affects the way in which the content can be consumed.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: So, accessibility of how the website presents itself to users is also something that we consider.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: With regard to the two-year framework, what we want to prevent in many cases, because a lot of times, community disputes verge on "he says", "I say".

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: And what we want to prevent is the return of vexatious claims made by parties.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: So, a two-year framework removes the potential for these vexatious claims to come back on a recurrent basis.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: And can the Member repeat the last point about end-to-end services again, if you do not mind?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to first declare that I am a practicing lawyer, serving on the Law Society's pro bono practice committee, as well as our Pro Bono SG's community legal clinics committee.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have two clarifications for Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The first is in relation to his explanations that the registration fees for the Wills Registry cannot be waived at this juncture and the reason is because it is to defray the fees for maintaining such a service.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I wish to propose, can we consider instead that waiving the fees but instead increase the search fees component.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fundamentally, the reason is because we really want to enable the Wills Registry to become a reliable and accurate repository where we are able to know exactly how many wills are accurate registered and done in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second suggestion or clarification is, to strengthen the comprehensive legacy planning, apart from the suggestions that I have made on Wills Registry and LPAs waivers, I wish to enquire whether can we also explore for the advanced medical directives, whether currently it is only allowed for the doctors to witness the signing of this legal instrument?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Akin to the same principle for registrations of LPAs, can we also work with the Ministry of Health to explore for the lawyers to do a comprehensive legacy planning which allows them to also witness the signing of an Advance Medical Directive (AMD)?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Chairman, I thank the Member for her clarifications.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: But in my own exchanges with, say, seniors on the ground, I think it is oftentimes far easier to broach a conversation on setting up an LPA and also drafting or talking about an Advance Care Plan.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: And then the AMD, which is actually much further down the line, is something that we can potentially look at after all these more upstream instruments have been addressed.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: On the Member's first question, do you mind repeating that again?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The first question has to do with what Minister has shared about support for the green transition, the digital economy, major regional infrastructure projects, and sports and entertainment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I was wondering if you could elaborate on that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And in line with that as well, whether there are stronger support and incentives for lawyers doing pro bono work?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overall, we have focused on Singapore being a hub.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I explained earlier, in dispute resolution, we have now one of the foremost number and the profile in terms of international institutions located in Singapore, so it made Singapore a hub for transactions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the stronger we are in terms of having an infrastructure to resolve disputes in a clear, fair, transparent manner, the more likely it is that investors will see opportunity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We take the same approach when it comes to IP as well as in international restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, these are areas in which we have built up a hub.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think this is an option and avenue for us to explore, and in fact, when I discuss with members of the Bar, with the Law Society, there are already lawyers who are interested in the areas, they practise in those areas and they are keen to elevate their practice areas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also had initial discussions with the Court of Arbitration for Sport with a view to seeing whether we can have collaboration with them, again, to bring it in here.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we do that on the same principle as what I have articulated for dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you have a system of being able to resolve disputes here, then you are more likely to be able to attract the entire ecosystem of investment and economic opportunity into Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, on that basis we have been working very closely with various practitioners, people who are interested in this area, and also, as I said, the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which represents one of the foremost global bodies on resolving sports disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To make one other point to Prof Goh's question, there is a degree to which IP can intersect with sport as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, WIPO is making this year's focus on World IP Day, the theme of in "IP and Sports".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Looking at sports, not just in terms of the resolving disputes around what you might do with transfers and the like, but also in terms of commercial marketing, licence rights, broadcast, image rights and the like.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, WIPO is working on promoting IP and sports, and we see an opportunity there, because, as I mentioned earlier, IP is one of our areas of focus for building the hub status in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My colleague Senior Minister of State Murali will talk a little bit more about green transition, but I will address your point on PDO.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I would like to assure the Member that we had catered for this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think they also find reward and value and purpose in the work that they do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, on that note, the Member's last point was what can else can we do?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We work with a variety of different organisations, including the Law Society, Pro Bono SG, with CLAS, and with the Bar in general, to promote giving back through pro bono work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And Pro Bono SG, CLAS and the work that we do with PDO are some examples of this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Here, the law's role is to shape how businesses operate, invest and structure transactions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And in this regard, IPOS has done studies on green trademarks and green economy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We also provide patent analytics insights to support the green economy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Over and above that, we are strengthening the ESG capabilities across the profession in partnership with key legal associations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, we supported initiatives such as the Singapore Corporate Counsel Association's (SCCA's) inaugural Sustainability Connect, a dedicated platform that brings together legal and sustainability professionals for knowledge exchange.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: SCCA Academy has also started to roll out ESG-focused training programmes, including a course delivered in partnership with Nanyang Technological University's Carbon Market Academy of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At the same time, the Law Society of Singapore and SAL have introduced a range of ESG-related training and thought leadership initiatives, equipping legal professionals with relevant capabilities.

text: We are approaching the end of guillotine time.

text: I know a few of you still have clarifications to make.

text: Priority will be given to those who have spoken on this earlier.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, please keep all clarifications and responses short.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But before that, I would like to thank him for the additional information that he has just given to us on the recent reappointment of the AG, which was information we did not have before.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, that was actually the thrust of my cut.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And the second is this: he mentioned that the current AG is required to continue managing some ongoing projects, which are quite complex.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is he saying now that the AG has become individually indispensable in the managing of these projects, there is no one being groomed to take over?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Because from a system point of view it sounds to me precarious, and in three years' time we might be facing the same argument again.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I cited a lot of public source information and data.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Wong's qualifications, his reputation, his CV and what he has achieved in both in public service as well as in private practice, I think it is really common knowledge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The ongoing projects that you mentioned and you seem to say that they are new, the fact that we have maritime boundary discussions, I think is not new.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have not gone into the sensitive materials because I cannot and I will not, but I think it suffices to say that we take this into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And on the Member's second question, it is not that any individual is indispensable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But at a given point in time, a multitude of factors are taken into account, as I said, including whether he is available, whether he is able to continue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Continuity is one factor, but it is not the only one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But taking all of this into account, factors such as what are the ongoing projects, his ability to contribute, the projects that are ongoing, the stature and reputation of the individual at hand, all of these are factors that we take into account in selecting the individual for the office.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As for the Member's first question, I am not going to go into whether there is a long list or a shortlist, but it suffices to say that we will consider this carefully, think about what the incumbent has done, whether there is a need to change at that point in time and if so, what are the options, and take all of these factors into consideration before deciding on making a recommendation to the President.

text: Members heard Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua outline some of the statistics.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai

text: I think in this day and age, businesses will need as many financing options in their arsenal.
