speaker: The Chairman
text: The hon Member Mr Vikram Nair had earlier officially applied for leave from Parliament for today because he has to attend a Court hearing.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Therefore, since Mr Vikram Nair is not here to withdraw his amendment, I will now put the amendment to a vote.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think the "Noes" have it, the "Noes" have it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head R of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I declare my interest as a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the years, MinLaw has played a critical role in strengthening the foundations of our legal system.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Today, I wish to focus on two aspects of the Ministry's work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, its initiatives aimed at enhancing Singaporeans' access to justice; and second, its efforts to grow Singapore as a trusted and leading hub for legal services.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It concerns the ability of ordinary Singaporeans and businesses to understand and assert their rights in a meaningful way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A strong legal system must serve not only large corporations and sophisticated litigants, but also parties who do not have deep pockets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, MinLaw has taken important steps in this direction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This included enhancements to the process of enforcing maintenance orders aimed at helping to litigants in person.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, in response to feedback that the existing process was expensive and difficult to navigate for the enforcement of judgments, steps were taken to simplify this process too, making enforcement more accessible and cost effective.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This taskforce will examine how the Government can better support such individuals who are at risk of offending or who may interact with the system, including accused persons and victims.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This reflects a holistic approach to justice which takes into account real circumstances and vulnerabilities of everyday Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Beyond structural reforms, we must also consider how technology is reshaping access to justice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The increasing availability of artificial intelligence (AI) tools presents an interesting conundrum.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the one hand, it empowers lay persons to conduct legal research on their own and has the potential to reduce legal costs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For one, lay persons may be tempted to rely on AI tools for legal advice but they may not realise that it is risky for them to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Court described this as a very serious matter, even for a lay person.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While there are ongoing initiatives to provide guidance to practising lawyers on the responsible use of AI, we should also consider providing guidance aimed at laypersons and litigants in person.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, there could be court notices or online resources aimed at lay persons which explain the limitations of AI tools.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: True access to justice must also include access to reliable and accurate information.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I turn now to the second aspect: the continued development of Singapore as an international hub for legal services.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This ambition cuts across multiple domains, including the strengthening of our dispute resolution system and institutions, such as the Singapore International Arbitration Centre, the Singapore International Mediation Centre and the Singapore International Commercial Court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Together, they form a complementary and attractive ecosystem for parties involved in international commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I wish to focus on two components of the vision to develop Singapore as an international legal hub: talent and technology.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The sustainability of legal practice has come into sharp focus in recent years, particularly with concerns about attrition and the long-term viability of private practice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my own practice and experience, I have noted a higher turnover amongst young lawyers in recent times, to the extent that young lawyers are leaving legal practice but remain in the legal profession, such as by going in-house.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not think that is a loss to the legal industry as a whole but in fact, helps the legal industry because a thriving pool of in-house talent is necessary for Singapore's success both as an economic and legal hub.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, we would like to keep young lawyers in private practice too.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Last year, the Ethics and Professional Standards Committee recommended that the Singapore Academy of Law develop a core set of workplace principles aimed at maintaining the sustainability of legal practice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most of these guidelines are well considered and it will be important for both law firms and other stakeholders to adopt practices which support professional development and well-being.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, technology, in particular the responsible and forward-looking use of AI.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The aim is to support the legal sector in harnessing opportunities, while navigating the challenges associated with using AI technology and being mindful of professional obligations in the delivery of legal services.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The impact of AI on the legal sector cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the honourable Chief Justice observed at TechLaw Fest 2025, generative AI (GenAI) will bring about a paradigm shift in the practice of law, and the legal sector must take this development seriously.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have seen reports both in Singapore and other jurisdictions, where lawyers have cited fictitious authorities in their submissions because they relied on AI tools.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am grateful for MinLaw's efforts on these fronts and look forward to the continued development of its initiatives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the MinLaw's Committee of Supply (COS) debate eight years ago, I spoke about the case of Canadian David Roach, who robbed StanChart Bank at Holland Village in 2016.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He fled to Thailand but could not be extradited to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was only two years later when Roach arrived in London enroute to Canada, that Singapore could make an extradition request to the United Kingdom (UK) government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While it certainly makes sense to have an ASEAN Extradition Treaty, I have two questions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What needs to be done before ratification, and has Singapore indicated its ratification?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, extradition arrangements need to take into account differences in legal systems and ASEAN countries are a mix of common law and civil law jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The region also has varying levels of corruption among public officials.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MinLaw has previously stated that there is a need to protect Singaporeans before agreeing to any extradition arrangements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, I declare that I am a practising lawyer and my areas of practice include estate matters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Government's national legacy planning campaign is commendable, and we should build on this momentum to help even more Singaporeans plan ahead.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) protects a donor while alive but ends upon death.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Then, a will is essential to legally express the testator's wishes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My first proposal is to waive the $50 registration fee and the $50 update fee for every will deposited with the Singapore Academy of Law's (SAL's) Wills Registry.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This fee deters many, unlike the successful LPA fee waiver by the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) that drove higher uptake.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Free registrations would encourage more deposits and transforming the Wills Registry into a reliable comprehensive database.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, we lack accurate data on how many Singaporeans have made wills, or whether a found will is the latest one.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A no fee system would address these gaps, just as the six-year LPA fee waiver did.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Second, as we encourage more will making, we must also strengthen safeguards.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Feedback from the lawyers and the public highlights concerning experiences with non-legal providers offering wills writing courses or services.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I raised a Parliamentary Question in October on regulating such businesses.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Ministry replied that wills and probate courses are not restricted to lawyers, but non lawyers cannot give legal advice or perform solicitor services.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Doing so risk criminal liability under the Legal Profession Act.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, can we fairly expect an average Singaporean to discern whether a course provider is rendering a legal advice or not.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Without registrations or mandatory professional indemnity insurance, vulnerable individuals risk relying on flawed advice with little recourse.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unscrupulous operators also risk tarnishing the reputation of our legal professions, which has upheld high standards for decades.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is our duty to protect Singaporeans from such risks and ensure legacy is both encouraged and safe.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Having observed residents attempting to navigate this process, I have seen how digital and financial requirements can be a deterrence and could account for the relatively low utilisation of this channel.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The mandatory pre-filing assessment requires a 17-question checklist, where the system repeatedly persuades applicants to seek alternative channels.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For residents who have already exhausted these channels, such persistence redirections can be frustrating.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Residents who do not know their neighbours name must pay $5.25 at the Integrated Land Information Service portal before even paying that $150 filing fee.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The English only interface and the assumption that all residents can manage PDF downloads and the digital evidence create massive barriers for those with lower digital literacy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: That was the extent of the information disclosed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Due to the high constitutional office of the AG and the significant powers he is entrusted with, I believe that the Prime Minister can and should be more forthcoming about the selection process for the AG.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Hence, I filed my cut with the Prime Minister's Office, but it had been redirected to MinLaw.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The AG occupies a uniquely sensitive position under our Constitution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He has the direct discretion to institute, conduct or discontinue any criminal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: For instance, he can decide to treat co-accused in the same case differently, or to let someone off with a warning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: His discretion is practically unfettered, unless he is found to have acted in bad faith or irrationally.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Unlike Judges who have to make pronouncements in open Court, his decisions need not be explained publicly and are not subject to appeal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The most the public can hope for is a voluntary media release from the AGC, giving reasons for prosecutorial discretion decisions that are deemed controversial.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: However, on the other, it is equally important for the AG to be consonant with public values so that he can act in the public interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: However, the appointment process required by the constitution is currently thin.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It merely says that the Prime Minister should consult the Chief Justice and the incumbent AG before making a recommendation to the President, and that the President has discretion to disagree.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: There is no requirement for public disclosure about any of these deliberations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: For example, in the present case, the AG has had a distinguished legal career in private practice, but the fact is that he will turn 75 at the end of this current term.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: On the other hand, there appear to be many qualified persons for the post.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It will also be instructive to know what experience each new AG brings to the post, in the light of the fact that the AG is expected to perform several roles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He is the public prosecutor and has the right of audience in any Court or tribunal in Singapore in precedence to others.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, experience in related areas of practice would be very useful.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The global commons is a shared space to be nurtured and contributed to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore, in its humble way, has consistently contributed to the international legal order with a degree of humility, with a degree of credibility and its strong sense of responsibility.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the appointment of Mr Darren Tang as Director-General of WIPO as well as his successful reappointment for a second term reflects the strength of Singapore's legal and IP ecosystem, and that our ability to produce thought leadership organically from within our own system and our own country.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also signals international confidence in Singapore's values and competence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition to WIPO, we should continue to try to play a small part in the global commons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This reflects our deep and humble commitment to the rule of law and peaceful dispute resolution in the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It speaks well of Singapore as a society that wants to contribute towards the good of the global commons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How will MinLaw continue to support opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans to make meaningful legal contributions internationally?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Singapore Convention on Mediation is an excellent piece of work showcasing Singapore's commitment to peaceful dispute resolution and the global commons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The legal service officers involved behind the convention and the Singapore Convention Week are to be commended.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, Singapore has become a trusted and preferred destination for mediation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many jurisdictions are now talking about the convention, thereby positioning Singapore as an ideal mediation hub.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here I declare that I am a partner in a legal private practice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To propel our status as a hub, Singapore will need infrastructure, such as exhibition facilities, to showcase mediation capabilities, breakout rooms, bilateral mediation hearing rooms as well as printers, laptops and screens for settlement agreements to be typed out.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I rise to speak on a subject that is close to my heart.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I am a practising advocate and solicitor, and I run my own law firm.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This means that a good number of practising lawyers are also small- to medium-sized business owners.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: For some time now, we have been witnessing a hollowing out of the legal profession, because young lawyers entering the profession are not staying and moving up in experience and seniority.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Some leave for better pay and challenging work in foreign firms.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The starting salaries for newly qualified lawyers in Singapore are considered pretty high, which is why staff remuneration now accounts for much of the operating costs of running a law practice.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Despite this, after a few years of practice, for many firms the exodus begins.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Even the large law firms are complaining that after investing in the training of their best and brightest, these young lawyers are leaving for foreign firms who pay even more.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Some may say, if lawyers are indeed able to find other employment, what is the issue?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: If we are unable to retain talent, this will have a profound implication in the longer term.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has a strong and trusted legal system that supports our economy, provides stability, builds investor confidence and attracts foreign investment.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It fosters a pro-business environment and positions Singapore as a leading global legal and financial hub.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: To continue delivering an excellent standard of legal services, we need to retain talent within legal practice, and we need advocates who have honed their craft over time who can assist our Courts on challenging cases and develop our own Singapore jurisprudence.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Our Chief Justice has announced a slew of initiatives to address these challenges and he will be co-leading with our Law Minister in setting the direction of the Future of the Legal Profession Committee to help the legal profession meet these challenges ahead.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Like many of my brethren at the Bar, I look forward to seeing what new plans will be rolled out.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We recognise that we all need to play our part, but we also the Government's support.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I want to acknowledge that MinLaw has pushed out programmes to help law firms embrace technological solutions to future-proof and deliver enhanced legal services.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: But embracing legal tech and AI can only do so much.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It could add to the stress that young lawyers are experiencing, wondering which aspect of their work will now be replaced and how they will cope with a redesign in their roles and responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The digital age has quickened the pace of practice and demands from clients have grown exponentially.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This is often what young lawyers complain about.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The revamping of our Rules of Court and the push towards mediation as an alternative mode of dispute resolution has also taken away some of the opportunities for Court advocacy and development of Court craft from our lawyers.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We may encourage lawyers to take pro bono cases to gain advocacy opportunities, but the realities of running a practice are such that paid work comes first.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Law firms who are prepared to give their lawyers protected time to take on access to justice cases, receive no financial incentive or tax breaks.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot simply focus on the firms that are prepared to make sizeable financial commitments toward modernising their practice.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It is my hope that in looking to future-proofing the legal profession and to retain and nurture talent, we will look at more than technological solutions, and understand that the issues relating to morale, career insecurity in the age of AI, financial and business stress are just as important.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as legal counsel in an accounting firm.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the Opening of Legal Year, the Chief Justice noted a key challenge: attrition driven by fundamental shifts in the practice.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is placing real pressure across the profession.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, our legal sector is more open than before.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With more international firms and regional competition, there are pressures to do more, faster and at lower cost.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These pressures will only intensify as AI becomes embedded in legal practice.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I wish to speak on three areas: maintaining a Singapore core; the evolving role of lawyers in the age of AI; and support for in-house counsel.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These proposals reflect a concern: sustaining a strong pipeline of local legal talent.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In essence, local firms build Singapore law capability, while foreign firms deepen foreign law expertise.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Ministry has yet to respond, with consultations just closed.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This raises a key tension: openness versus preserving a Singapore core.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Some of the young lawyers and law students that I have spoken to shared their anxieties with me.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are not sure where they fit in the larger plans that the Ministry has for the legal profession.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How does the Ministry intend to balance market forces with regulation to protect that core?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And how will the Ministry ensure Singapore lawyers continue to access high-value international work?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, on the evolving roles of lawyers in the age of AI.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They did not grow up with AI, and it may not come naturally to them to use AI.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must consider carefully the impact of AI on our mid-career professionals.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What is the Ministry's plan to ensure that senior and mid-career lawyers are equipped to learn AI skills, reskill and redesign their job roles?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, how do we train young lawyers, when AI can already do so much that juniors do today, but faster?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Junior lawyers must learn to think like lawyers, grounded in legal rigour.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But they must also interpret technology, review AI outputs critically and exercise human judgement in complex cases.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How does the Ministry plan to support new training pathways so young lawyers build fundamentals, while learning to work alongside AI?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We need a sector-wide approach to job redesign so that the whole profession moves together.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I encourage the Ministry to take the lead.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In-house counsels play a critical role in supporting business and strengthening Singapore's attractiveness as a regional hub.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will the Ministry support access to AI tools and target upskilling so that in-house legal counsel can continue to deliver value in an AI-enabled economy?

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, as a society and economy, we must harness the potential of AI to drive innovation and progress.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan (Nee Soon)
text: But we also must ensure that the systems that are in place have to safeguard what makes us human, such as the unique contributions of our creatives that shape our national culture and identity.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan (Nee Soon)
text: The training and use of GenAI continues to raise concerns among stakeholders, particularly those in the creative sectors.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan (Nee Soon)
text: These included approaches to improve transparency on how copyrighted material is used for AI training and ways to strengthen the control that rights-holders have over their material.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan (Nee Soon)
text: Would MinLaw and the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) be able to provide an update on the work done, and how the Government has responded or will respond to these concerns?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest that I am a practising lawyer.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In March 2025, a report was jointly commissioned by MinLaw, the Economic Development Board and Enterprise Singapore, and independently researched by PriceWaterhouseCoopers (PwC), titled "Sustainability Ready Singapore Lawyers".

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It identified environmental, social and governance (ESG) as a key area of growth in our legal sector.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is timely as ESG advisory is becoming increasingly relevant in green finance, carbon markets and sustainability reporting.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: However, secondments may not be feasible for all firms, particularly small and medium-sized practices.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I would therefore like to seek an update on the development of ESG capabilities within our legal sector.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Would the Minister provide a snapshot of this programme, including the level of uptake and feedback thus far?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It would also be helpful to understand where these lawyers have been seconded to, given that this remains a nascent area of growth.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In addition, what other pathways are being developed to support lawyers who are unable to participate in secondments?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For example, are there structured ESG training frameworks, accreditation programmes, short industry attachments or collaboration platforms with financial institutions and sustainability professionals?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Chair, I start by declaring my interest as the president of a National Sport Association.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, Singapore has positioned itself as a global destination for major sporting and cultural entertainment events, hosting the Singapore Grand Prix, the Women's Tennis Association and most recently, the World Aquatics Championships, alongside major concerts and entertainment productions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: As we build on this trajectory, there may be scope to consider how our legal and land-use architecture can further support Singapore's evolution into a regional sports and entertainment hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Legal certainty is often a key consideration for organisers and rights holders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But global ambition must ultimately rest on strong local participation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In a land-scarce and tropical environment, usability is often constrained by heat and rain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And could structural shading or lightweight roofing for open-air spaces be more systematically considered to enhance climate resilience and expand all-day, all-weather use?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we want world-class events, we must also ensure world-class everyday access.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Both events and daily access are essential to a thriving sports, arts and cultural entertainment ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, beyond the broader discussion on enterprise competitiveness, I would like to raise two specific issues – accelerating intellectual property (IP) commercialisation for SMEs and strengthening IP financing.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: On commercialisation, many SMEs struggle to translate publicly funded research into market-ready products.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The gap is often not invention, but execution – bridging laboratory innovation to deployable solutions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: There have been recommendations to strengthen structured attachments of scientists and researchers to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) – not merely short-term consultancy, but deeper co-development partnerships.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such models can accelerate technology transfer, reduce execution risk and build internal innovation capability within enterprises.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: On financing, IP remains difficult to value and underwrite.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Without tangible collateral, SMEs often struggle to leverage their IP for expansion capital.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we want to move from research excellence to enterprise scale, commercialisation pathways and financing frameworks must evolve alongside IP creation.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, the rule of law is one of Singapore's greatest strengths.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It gives investors confidence, keeps our society stable and helps Singaporeans trust our system.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But for it to stay strong, it must remain accessible to our people and respected around the world.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I would like to speak on two areas: first, strengthening access to justice through civil legal aid and socio-legal support; second, strengthening Singapore's position as a trusted global intellectual property hub in a fast-changing technological world.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, in a written reply to a Parliamentary Question on 26 September 2025, the Minister explained the current framework for civil legal aid.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The Legal Aid Bureau provides support to Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents who meet the means test and the merits test.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: There is also flexibility through the Means Test Panel for deserving cases.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Those who do not qualify can turn to Community Law Centres, run by Pro Bono SG, as well as schemes such as the Family Justice Support Scheme and the Ad Hoc Pro Bono Scheme.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But Chairman, the question is whether this is enough in today's more complex and costly legal environment.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Civil cases today, especially family, employment and debt matters, are becoming more complicated.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Legal costs have increased and processes are becoming more demanding.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Are there plans to review it regularly to keep pace with economic conditions?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Second, while the Means Test Panel provides flexibility, how often is it used?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: And is it enough to help those who fall just outside the eligibility criteria?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Third, for those who rely on Community Law Centres and pro bono services, is there enough capacity, especially for family and employment disputes?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, as cases become more complex, has the Ministry considered strengthening early legal advice and triage so people can get proper guidance before problems escalate?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I will touch on growing Singapore as a trusted global IP hub.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's future competitiveness depends increasingly on intangible assets such as intellectual property and innovation.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Under the Singapore IP Strategy 2030, we have set out a strong vision.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But as technology advances, especially in AI, IP policy is no longer just legal policy.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: This clarity will be important for trust and confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, cost-of-living pressures have tightened budgets for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And when life hits, retrenchment, separation, caregiving strain, debt and legal problems do not come with a warning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In these moments, access to justice cannot become what we call a justice tax.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For lower-income Singaporeans, legal aid is sometimes not optional.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is the difference between getting timely advice and being forced to navigate complex processes alone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When families are already stretched, they should not be priced out of basic legal protection.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But accessibility is not just about whether a scheme exists.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is whether residents can actually use it when they are under stress, worried about bills, juggling work, caring for family and trying to keep life together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If the system feels out of reach, people delay, disputes worsen and the eventual outcome is often more painful for everyone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They may fall outside the legal aid threshold, but they, too, struggle to afford private legal fees.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are asking not to be stuck in a gap where they are told they do not qualify yet cannot realistically pay for help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This matters because when the squeezed middle cannot access advice early, problems escalate, creating avoidable stress for families and greater strain on the system later.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, Sir, I have two questions for the Minister.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Given cost-of-living concerns, how will the Ministry continue to ensure that legal aid remains accessible to lower-income Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare that I am a lawyer in private practice for both my cuts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Disputes are distressing but an inevitable consequence of personal and commercial interactions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If unresolved, some disputes end up before the Civil Courts or tribunals for resolution.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If you are an individual, legal proceedings can often be a frustrating and stressful process.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: And yet, even after you obtain a judgment in your favour, it does not necessarily mean that you have succeeded.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: There is still the matter of enforcing the judgment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The enforcement process can sometimes be an equal, if not more, trying process.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This included proposals for Civil Judgment Enforcement Officers who can assist to better locate debtors' assets.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: These reforms were slated to also apply to tribunals such as the Employment Claims Tribunal and Small Claims Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the domain of family disputes, the Maintenance Enforcement Process is a major step forward.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I invite the Minister to share an update with this House on the proposed enhancements to the civil enforcement process, including the proposed introduction of Civil Judgment Enforcement Officers, and the progress and outcomes of the Maintenance Enforcement Process.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Legal fees can be daunting for families and individuals.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The pressure is aggravated when it involves family-related legal matters that are impossible to avoid.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: At COS 2025, the Minister shared that the means testing criteria for civil legal aid were revised in 2024 to ensure legal aid continues to be accessible to Singaporeans who need assistance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the area of civil law, based on experience at our Potong Pasir Community Legal Clinic over the past 12 years, less privileged families often reach out to seek assistance in probate matters such as the procurement of letters of administration or deputyship applications under the Mental Capacity Act when a member of the family, often a senior, suffers from mental capacity medical conditions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: These families are often slightly above the threshold for legal aid but face financial challenges to retain lawyers to advise and deal with these matters on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: There are aspects of these matters that could result in frustrating and trying issues for families if left unresolved.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Deputyship to act on behalf of a senior in the family, for example, is important for families to make decisions for the senior and to have access, and be able to manage his or her assets.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I invite the Minister to share with this House, if the Ministry has plans to review the means testing threshold for civil legal aid and if the Ministry will consider a tiered approached to means testing for legal aid in areas of law, such as probate-related and/or deputyship applications to allow more Singaporean families to benefit from legal assistance for such legal matters.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: For many Singaporeans, especially small businesses and middle-income households, obtaining judgment is only half the battle.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But without enforcement, it is only a piece of paper.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Today, enforcement can be costly, slow and uncertain.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Creditors must spend more time and money tracing assets, initiating further applications and navigating complex procedures.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: When debtors conceal assets or ignore Court orders, the burden falls back on the successful party.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This is not just inconvenient; it is destabilising.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: For a small business, delayed recovery can affect cash flow and survival.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: For individuals, it prolongs stress and financial strain.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: If Court orders are ignored without consequences, confidence in the rule of law is weakened.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Our justice system must not only decide cases fairly.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, access to justice is not only about enforcement.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We are in a period of cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: While legal aid schemes are valuable, many lower- and middle-income Singaporeans may fall into a difficult gap – earning too much to qualify, yet too little to afford sustained legal representation.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Access to justice should not depend on one’s ability to pay substantial upfront legal fees.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Eligibility thresholds and coverage frameworks must keep pace with living costs.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, more can be done to support litigants-in-person.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Simplified procedures, clearer guidance and enhanced assisted self-help tools can reduce costs while preserving fairness.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Second, will further procedural simplifications or assisted self-help mechanisms be introduced to ease the burden on middle-income litigants?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This policy cut is modest in amount but serious in purpose.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And the doors of justice must remain meaningfully open.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Strengthening enforcement and expanding accessibility are not optional refinements.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: They are foundational to public confidence in our legal system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Singapore Land Authority plays an important role in unlocking the value of state land for community use.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As a sportsman, I have personally seen with immense joy how underutilised spaces, such as areas under flyovers, can be transformed into safe and vibrant places for sport and recreation, whether for pickleball, futsal, badminton, tennis or even archery and possibly even hockey.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But could we go beyond flyovers, empty school fields, old black and white bungalow spaces, old colonial terraces and more?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: All these are ripe for use for sport, football, archery, hockey, pickleball, dance, floorball and art galleries — Thank you.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan (Nee Soon)
text: The Land Betterment Charge was introduced in 2022 to capture part of the land value uplift that accrues to landowners when the Government enhances development potential through planning decisions.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan (Nee Soon)
text: This is important because it reflects our commitment to collective benefit.
